questions.q: Figure represents the extension ($\Delta l$) of a wire of length $1$ meter, suspended from the ceiling of the room at one end with a load $W$ connected to the other end. If the cross-sectional area of the wire is $10^{-5}$ m$^2$ then the Young's modulus of the wire is __________ N/m$^2$.
questions.solution:
From the given graph, we can observe that for a load $W = 20$ N, the extension is $\Delta l = 2 \times 10^{-4}$ m.

The formula for Young's modulus $Y$ is:

$Y = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \dfrac{W / A}{\Delta l / L} = \dfrac{W L}{A \Delta l}$

Given:
Length of the wire, $L = 1$ m
Cross-sectional area, $A = 10^{-5}$ m$^2$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$Y = \dfrac{20 \times 1}{10^{-5} \times 2 \times 10^{-4}}$

$Y = \dfrac{20}{2 \times 10^{-9}}$

$Y = 10 \times 10^9 = 1.0 \times 10^{10}$ N/m$^2$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{10}$

questions.q: A lift of mass $1600$ kg is supported by thick iron wire. If the maximum stress which the wire can withstand is $4 \times 10^8$ N/m$^2$ and its radius is $4$ mm, then maximum acceleration the lift can take is _______ m/s$^2$. (take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$ and $\pi = 3.14$)
questions.solution:
Maximum stress $\sigma_{max} = 4 \times 10^8$ N/m$^2$

Radius of wire $r = 4 \times 10^{-3}$ m

Mass of lift $m = 1600$ kg

Maximum tension the wire can withstand is given by:

$T_{max} = \sigma_{max} \times \pi r^2$

$T_{max} = 4 \times 10^8 \times 3.14 \times (4 \times 10^{-3})^2$

$T_{max} = 4 \times 10^8 \times 3.14 \times 16 \times 10^{-6} = 20096$ N

When the lift accelerates upwards with maximum acceleration $a$, the tension in the wire is:

$T_{max} = m(g + a)$

$20096 = 1600(10 + a)$

$10 + a = \dfrac{20096}{1600} = 12.56$

$a = 12.56 - 10 = 2.56$ m/s$^2$

Answer: $2.56$

questions.q: The two wires $A$ and $B$ of equal cross-section but of different materials are joined together. The ratio of Young's modulus of wire $A$ and wire $B$ is $20/11$. When the joined wire is kept under certain tension the elongations in the wires $A$ and $B$ are equal. If the length of wire $A$ is $2.2$ m, then the length of wire $B$ is _______ m.
questions.solution:
Given that the wires have equal cross-sectional area $A$ and are under the same tension $F$, the elongation $\Delta L$ is given by:

$\Delta L = \dfrac{F L}{A Y}$

Since the elongations in both wires are equal ($\Delta L_A = \Delta L_B$):

$\dfrac{F L_A}{A Y_A} = \dfrac{F L_B}{A Y_B}$

$\dfrac{L_A}{Y_A} = \dfrac{L_B}{Y_B}$

$L_B = L_A \times \dfrac{Y_B}{Y_A}$

Substituting the given values $L_A = 2.2$ m and $\dfrac{Y_A}{Y_B} = \dfrac{20}{11}$:

$L_B = 2.2 \times \dfrac{11}{20}$

$L_B = \dfrac{24.2}{20} = 1.21$ m

Answer: $1.21$

questions.q:
A copper wire of length $3\text{ m}$ is stretched by $3\text{ mm}$ by applying an external force. The volume of the wire is $600 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$. The elastic potential energy stored in the wire in stretched condition would be _______ J.
(Given Young modulus of copper $= 1.1 \times 10^{11}\text{ N/m}^2$)
questions.solution:
Given parameters:
$L = 3\text{ m}$
$\Delta L = 3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$
$V = 600 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$
$Y = 1.1 \times 10^{11}\text{ N/m}^2$

Strain is given by:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-3}}{3} = 10^{-3}$

Elastic potential energy stored in the wire is:
$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{Stress} \times \text{Strain} \times \text{Volume}$

Since $\text{Stress} = Y \times \text{Strain}$:
$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times Y \times (\text{Strain})^2 \times V$

Substituting the values:
$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (1.1 \times 10^{11}) \times (10^{-3})^2 \times (600 \times 10^{-6})$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.1 \times 10^{11} \times 10^{-6} \times 600 \times 10^{-6}$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.1 \times 600 \times 10^{-1}$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 66 = 33\text{ J}$

Answer: $33$

It depends only on the nature of the material and its temperature, and is independent of the dimensions of the wire such as length $L$ and radius $r$.

Therefore, when the radius and length of the steel wire are doubled, its Young's modulus remains unchanged.

questions.q:
Two wires as shown in the figure below, made of steel and have breaking stress of $12 \times 10^8$ N/m$^2$. Area of cross-section of upper wire is $0.008$ cm$^2$ and of lower wire is $0.004$ cm$^2$. The maximum mass that can be added to pan without breaking any wire is _____ kg.
(take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the maximum mass that can be added to the pan be $m$.

The breaking stress for both wires is $\sigma_{max} = 12 \times 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$.

For the upper wire:
Area of cross-section, $A_u = 0.008 \text{ cm}^2 = 8 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$
Maximum tension the upper wire can withstand is:
$T_{u,max} = \sigma_{max} \times A_u = (12 \times 10^8) \times (8 \times 10^{-7}) = 960 \text{ N}$
The total mass supported by the upper wire is $(30 + 10 + m) = (40 + m) \text{ kg}$.
Tension in the upper wire, $T_u = (40 + m)g = (40 + m) \times 10$
To avoid breaking the upper wire:
$(40 + m) \times 10 \le 960$
$40 + m \le 96 \implies m \le 56 \text{ kg}$

For the lower wire:
Area of cross-section, $A_l = 0.004 \text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$
Maximum tension the lower wire can withstand is:
$T_{l,max} = \sigma_{max} \times A_l = (12 \times 10^8) \times (4 \times 10^{-7}) = 480 \text{ N}$
The total mass supported by the lower wire is $(10 + m) \text{ kg}$.
Tension in the lower wire, $T_l = (10 + m)g = (10 + m) \times 10$
To avoid breaking the lower wire:
$(10 + m) \times 10 \le 480$
$10 + m \le 48 \implies m \le 38 \text{ kg}$

To ensure neither wire breaks, the added mass $m$ must satisfy both conditions. Therefore, the maximum mass that can be added is the smaller of the two values:
$m = 38 \text{ kg}$

Answer: $38$

questions.q: A cube has side length $5$ cm and modulus of rigidity $10^5$ N/m$^2$. The displacement produced by a force of $10$ N in the upper face of cube is _____ mm.
questions.solution:
Given:
Side length of the cube, $L = 5$ cm $= 0.05$ m
Modulus of rigidity, $\eta = 10^5$ N/m$^2$
Force applied on the upper face, $F = 10$ N

Area of the upper face, $A = L^2 = (0.05)^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^2$

Shear stress is given by:
$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{10}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 4000$ N/m$^2$

Shear strain is given by:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{L}$

Modulus of rigidity is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain:
$\eta = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta x/L}$

Rearranging for displacement $\Delta x$:
$\Delta x = \dfrac{F \cdot L}{A \cdot \eta}$

Substituting the values:
$\Delta x = \dfrac{10 \times 0.05}{2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^5}$

$\Delta x = \dfrac{0.5}{250} = 0.002$ m

Converting to millimeters:
$\Delta x = 0.002 \times 1000 = 2$ mm

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal string $A$ is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass $M$. Second block having mass $2M$ is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string $B$. The area of cross sections of strings $A$ and $B$ are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of $A$ to $B$ is $2$ and the ratio of their Young's moduli $(Y_A/Y_B)$ is $0.5$. The ratio of elongations in $A$ to $B$ is ______.
questions.solution:
Tension in string $B$ is due to the block of mass $2M$:

$T_B = 2Mg$

Tension in string $A$ is due to both blocks of mass $M$ and $2M$:

$T_A = Mg + 2Mg = 3Mg$

The elongation in a string is given by Hooke's law as $\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY}$.

The ratio of elongations in string $A$ to string $B$ is:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B} = \left(\dfrac{T_A}{T_B}\right) \left(\dfrac{L_A}{L_B}\right) \left(\dfrac{A_B}{A_A}\right) \left(\dfrac{Y_B}{Y_A}\right)$

Given that $\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = 2$, $\dfrac{A_B}{A_A} = 1$, and $\dfrac{Y_A}{Y_B} = 0.5 \Rightarrow \dfrac{Y_B}{Y_A} = 2$.

Substituting the values into the ratio equation:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B} = \left(\dfrac{3Mg}{2Mg}\right) \times (2) \times (1) \times (2)$

$\dfrac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B} = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 4 = 6$

Answer: $6$

questions.q: The increase in the pressure required to decrease the volume $(\Delta V)$ of water is $6.3 \times 10^7$ N/m$^2$. The percentage decrease in the volume is _____. (Bulk modulus of water $= 2.1 \times 10^9$ N/m$^2$.)
questions.solution:
Bulk modulus is given by $B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}}$

The fractional decrease in volume is $-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{\Delta P}{B}$

Substituting the given values:

$-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{6.3 \times 10^7}{2.1 \times 10^9} = 3 \times 10^{-2}$

The percentage decrease in volume is $\left(-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}\right) \times 100$

Percentage decrease $= 3 \times 10^{-2} \times 100 = 3\%$

Answer: $3\%$

questions.q: A string $A$ of length $0.314$ m and Young's modulus $2 \times 10^{10}$ N/m$^2$ is connected to another string $B$ of length and Young's modulus both twice of those of $A$. This series combination of strings is then suspended from a rigid support and its free end is fixed to a load of mass $0.8$ kg. The net change in length of the combination is _____ mm. (radius of both the strings is $0.2$ mm and acceleration due to gravity $= 10$ m/s$^2$) (Mass of both strings is to be neglected as compared to the mass of load)
questions.solution:
Given:
Length of string A, $L_A = 0.314$ m
Young's modulus of string A, $Y_A = 2 \times 10^{10}$ N/m$^2$
Radius of both strings, $r = 0.2$ mm $= 2 \times 10^{-4}$ m
Length of string B, $L_B = 2L_A = 0.628$ m
Young's modulus of string B, $Y_B = 2Y_A = 4 \times 10^{10}$ N/m$^2$
Mass of load, $m = 0.8$ kg
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10$ m/s$^2$

Tension in both strings, $T = mg = 0.8 \times 10 = 8$ N

Cross-sectional area of both strings:
$A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (2 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-8}$ m$^2$

Elongation in string A:
$\Delta L_A = \dfrac{T L_A}{A Y_A}$
$\Delta L_A = \dfrac{8 \times 0.314}{3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-8} \times 2 \times 10^{10}}$
$\Delta L_A = \dfrac{8 \times 0.314}{8 \times 3.14 \times 10^2} = \dfrac{0.1}{10^2} = 10^{-3}$ m $= 1$ mm

Elongation in string B:
$\Delta L_B = \dfrac{T L_B}{A Y_B}$
$\Delta L_B = \dfrac{8 \times (2 \times 0.314)}{A \times (2 Y_A)} = \dfrac{T L_A}{A Y_A} = 1$ mm

Net change in length of the combination:
$\Delta L = \Delta L_A + \Delta L_B = 1 + 1 = 2$ mm

Answer: $2$

The diameter of a wire measured by a screw gauge of least count $0.001$ cm is $0.08$ cm. The length measured by a scale of least count $0.1$ cm is $150$ cm. When a weight of $100$ N is applied to the wire, the extension in length is $0.5$ cm, measured by a micrometer of least count $0.001$ cm. The error in the measured Young's modulus is $\alpha \times 10^9$ N/m$^2$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
(Ignore the contribution of the load to Young's modulus error calculation)
questions.solution:
The formula for Young's modulus is given by:

$Y = \dfrac{F L_0}{A \Delta L} = \dfrac{4 F L_0}{\pi d^2 \Delta L}$

Substituting the given values into the formula:

$Y = \dfrac{4 \times 100 \times 1.5}{\pi \times (0.08 \times 10^{-2})^2 \times (0.5 \times 10^{-2})}$

$Y = \dfrac{600}{\pi \times 64 \times 10^{-8} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15}{8\pi} \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$

The relative error in Young's modulus is:

$\dfrac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \dfrac{\Delta L_0}{L_0} + 2\dfrac{\Delta d}{d} + \dfrac{\Delta (\Delta L)}{\Delta L}$

Substituting the least counts as absolute errors and the measured values:

$\dfrac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \dfrac{0.1}{150} + 2 \times \dfrac{0.001}{0.08} + \dfrac{0.001}{0.5}$

$\dfrac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \dfrac{1}{1500} + \dfrac{1}{40} + \dfrac{1}{500}$

$\dfrac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \dfrac{2 + 75 + 6}{3000} = \dfrac{83}{3000}$

The absolute error in Young's modulus is:

$\Delta Y = Y \times \dfrac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \left(\dfrac{15}{8\pi} \times 10^{11}\right) \times \dfrac{83}{3000}$

$\Delta Y = \dfrac{15 \times 83}{24000 \pi} \times 10^{11} = \dfrac{83}{1600 \pi} \times 10^{11} = \dfrac{83}{16\pi} \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$\Delta Y = \dfrac{83}{16 \times 3.14} \times 10^9 = \dfrac{83}{50.24} \times 10^9 \approx 1.65 \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$

Comparing this with $\alpha \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$, we get $\alpha = 1.65$.

Answer: $1.65$

questions.q: A uniform wire of length $l$ of weight $w$ is suspended from the roof with a weight of $W$ at the other end. The stress in the wire at $\dfrac{l}{3}$ distance from the top is $\left(\dfrac{W}{A} + \dfrac{2}{\gamma}\dfrac{w}{A}\right)$, where, $A$ is the cross sectional area of the wire. The value of $\gamma$ is _______.
questions.solution:
Let $T$ be the tension in the wire at a distance $\dfrac{l}{3}$ from the top.

The length of the wire below this point is $l - \dfrac{l}{3} = \dfrac{2l}{3}$.

The weight of this lower part of the wire is $\dfrac{w}{l} \times \dfrac{2l}{3} = \dfrac{2w}{3}$.

The total downward force (tension $T$) at this point is the sum of the weight $W$ attached at the bottom and the weight of the lower part of the wire:

$T = W + \dfrac{2w}{3}$

The stress at this point is given by the tension divided by the cross-sectional area $A$:

$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{T}{A} = \dfrac{W + \dfrac{2w}{3}}{A} = \dfrac{W}{A} + \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{w}{A}$

Comparing this with the given expression for stress, $\dfrac{W}{A} + \dfrac{2}{\gamma}\dfrac{w}{A}$, we get:

$\gamma = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.q: Two wires $A$ and $B$ made of different materials of lengths 6.0 cm and 5.4 cm, respectively and area of cross sections $3.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ and $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$, respectively are stretched by the same magnitude under a given load. The ratio of the Young's modulus of $A$ to that of $B$ is $x: 3$. The value of $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Young's modulus: $Y = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} = \frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$.
When the same force is applied and both wires stretch by the same extension $\Delta L$, the ratio of Young's moduli is:
$\frac{Y_A}{Y_B} = \frac{F/A_A}{\Delta L/L_A} \times \frac{\Delta L/L_B}{F/A_B} = \frac{A_B}{A_A} \times \frac{L_A}{L_B}$
$=\frac{4.5 \times 10^{-5}}{3.0 \times 10^{-5}} \times \frac{6.0}{5.4} = 1.5 \times \frac{10}{9} = \frac{5}{3}$.
Therefore $x : 3 = 5 : 3$, giving $x = 5$.

questions.q: The strain-stress plot for materials $A, B, C$ and $D$ is shown in the figure. Which material has the largest Young's modulus ?
questions.solution:
Young's modulus ($Y$) is defined as the ratio of stress to strain: $Y = \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}$.
In the given graph, the y-axis represents strain and the x-axis represents stress.
The slope of the line in a strain-stress graph is given by $m = \frac{\text{strain}}{\text{stress}}$.
Therefore, $Y = \frac{1}{\text{slope}}$.
To have the largest Young's modulus, the material must have the smallest slope in the strain-stress plot.
From the figure, line $C$ has the smallest angle with the stress axis (x-axis), meaning it has the minimum slope.
Since $Y \propto \frac{1}{\text{slope}}$, material $C$ has the largest Young's modulus.

questions.q: A sample of a liquid is kept at 1 atm. It is compressed to 5 atm which leads to change of volume of $0.8 \mathrm{~cm}^3$. If the bulk modulus of the liquid is 2 GPa , the initial volume of the liquid was _______ litre. $\left(\right.$ Take $\left.1 \mathrm{~atm}=10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given, Initial pressure of liquid $\left(P_i\right)=1 \mathrm{~atm}$
Final pressure of liquid $\left(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\right)=5 \mathrm{~atm}$
Change in pressure $(\mathrm{dP})=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}}=4 \mathrm{~atm}$
$=4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}$
Change in volume $(\mathrm{dV})=-0.8 \mathrm{~cm}^3$
Bulk modulus $(B)=2 \times 10^9 \mathrm{~Pa}$
Now, $B=\frac{-d P}{(d V / V)} \Rightarrow V=-B\left(\frac{d V}{d P}\right)$
$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & V=-2 \times 10^9 \times \frac{\left(-0.8 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{4 \times 10^5} \\ & =4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3=4 \text{ litre }
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Two wires A and B are made of same material having ratio of lengths $\frac{L_A}{L_B}=\frac{1}{3}$ and their diameters ratio $\frac{d_A}{d_B}=2$. If both the wires are stretched using same force, what would be the ratio of their respective elongations?
questions.solution:
$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$
$\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}$
Given, $F_A=F_B$ and $Y_A=Y_B$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{B}}^2}{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{A}}^2}\right)=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)^2$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{12}$

The volume contraction of a solid copper cube of edge length 10 cm , when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of $7 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~Pa}$, would be ____ $\mathrm{mm}^3$.
(Given bulk modulus of copper $=1.4 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}$ )

questions.q: The increase in pressure required to decrease the volume of a water sample by $0.2 \%$ is $\mathrm{P} \times 10^5 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$. Bulk modulus of water is $2.15 \times 10^9 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$. The value of P is $\ldots\ldots$
questions.solution:
Since bulk modulus is given as
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{B}=\frac{-\Delta \mathrm{P}}{\left(\frac{\Delta \mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{~V}}\right)} \\
& 2.15 \times 10^9=\frac{-\Delta \mathrm{P}}{-\left(\frac{0.2}{100}\right)} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{P}=2.15 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} \\
& =4.3 \times 10^6=43 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2
\end{aligned}$

One end of a metal wire is fixed to a ceiling and a load of $2kg$ hangs from the other end. A similar wire is attached to the bottom of the load and another load of $1kg$ hangs from this lower wire. Then the ratio of longitudinal strain of upper wire to that of the lower wire will be

[Area of cross section of wire $= 0 . 005{cm}^{2}, Y = 2 \times {10}^{11}N{m}^{- 2}$ and $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$]
questions.solution:
As we know, change in length is given by $\DeltaL = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$

Therefore, strain required $\dfrac{\DeltaL}{L} = \dfrac{F}{AY}$

Now the ratio will be, $\dfrac{\dfrac{\Delta{L}_{1}}{{L}_{1}}}{\dfrac{\Delta{L}_{2}}{{L}_{2}}} = \dfrac{{F}_{1}}{{F}_{2}} = \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$

questions.q: A wire of length $L$ and radius $r$ is clamped at one end. If its other end is pulled by a force $F$, its length increases by $l$. If the radius of the wire and the applied force both are reduced to half of their original values keeping original length constant, the increase in length will become:
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire, in the first case, can be written as

$Y = \dfrac{\dfrac{F}{\pi{r}^{2}}}{\dfrac{l}{L}} . . . \left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

$F = Y\pi{r}^{2} \times \dfrac{l}{L} . . . \left(2\right)$

For the second case, the Young's modulus is given by

$Y = \dfrac{\dfrac{F / 2}{\pi{r}^{2} / 4}}{\dfrac{l '}{L}} . . . \left(3\right)$

From equation (3), it follows that

$F = Y\dfrac{l '}{L} \times 2 \times \dfrac{\pi{r}^{2}}{4} . . . \left(4\right)$

From equations (2) and (4), it implies that

$Y\pi{r}^{2} \times \dfrac{l}{L} = Y\dfrac{l '}{L} \times 2 \times \dfrac{\pi{r}^{2}}{4} ⇒ l ' = 2l$

questions.q: Two metallic wires $P$ and $Q$ have same volume and are made up of same material. If their area of cross sections are in the ratio $4: 1$ and force ${F}_{1}$ is applied to $P$, an extension of $∆ l$ is produced. The force which is required to produce same extension in $Q$ is ${F}_{2}$. The value of $\dfrac{{F}_{1}}{{F}_{2}}$ is ______.
questions.solution:
The formula for Young's modulus is given by

$\begin{cases}Y & = & \dfrac{\dfrac{F}{A}}{\dfrac{∆ l}{l}} \\ & = & \dfrac{Fl}{A ∆ l}\end{cases}$

From above equation, it follows that

$\Deltal = \dfrac{Fl}{AY} . . . \left(1\right)$

Again, volume of the wire is given by

$V = Al ⇒ l = \dfrac{V}{A}$

Hence, from equation (1),

$∆ l = \dfrac{FV}{{A}^{2}Y} . . . \left(2\right)$

As, $Y$ and $V$ is the same for both the wires,

$∆ l ∝ \dfrac{F}{{A}^{2}}$

Hence, for two wires, it can be written that

$\dfrac{∆ {l}_{1}}{∆ {l}_{2}} = \dfrac{{F}_{1}}{{A}_{1}^{2}} \times {A}_{2}^{2}{F}_{2} . . . \left(3\right)$

As $∆ {l}_{1} = ∆ {l}_{2}$, from equation (3), it follows that

${F}_{1}{A}_{2}^{2} = {F}_{2}{A}_{1}^{2} ⇒ \dfrac{{F}_{1}}{{F}_{2}} = {A}_{1}^{2}{A}_{2}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{4}{1}\right)}^{2} = 16$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R)
Assertion (A) : The property of body, by virtue of which it tends to regain its original shape when the external force is removed, is Elasticity.
Reason (R) : The restoring force depends upon the bonded inter atomic and inter molecular force of solid.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Elasticity is the ability of a material to deform under stress and then return to its original shape when the stress is removed.

The restoring force in elastic materials is associated with the inter-atomic or inter-molecular forces that act to bring the atoms or molecules back to their original positions when the material is deformed. When an external force is applied to a material, it causes a displacement of atoms or molecules from their equilibrium positions. questions.q: The elastic potential energy stored in a steel wire of length $20m$ stretched through $2cm$ is $80J .$ The cross sectional area of the wire is _____ ${mm}^{2} .$ (Given, $Y = 2 . 0 \times {10}^{11}N{m}^{– 2}$)
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material is given by

$\begin{cases}Y & = & \dfrac{stress}{strain} \\ & = & \dfrac{stress}{\dfrac{∆ l}{L}} . . . \left(1\right)\end{cases}$

The formula to calculate the potential energy $\left(U\right)$ stored into the wire is given by

$\begin{cases}U & = & \dfrac{1}{2} \times stress \times strain \times volume \\ & = & \dfrac{1}{2} \times stress \times \dfrac{∆ l}{L} \times A \times L \\ & = & \dfrac{1}{2} \times stress \times A \times ∆ l . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

From equation (1) and equation (2), it can be written that

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times Y \times \dfrac{{\left(∆ l\right)}^{2}}{L} \times A . . . \left(3\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) and solve to calculate the required cross-sectional area of the wire.

$\begin{cases}80J & = & \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 . 0 \times {10}^{11}{Nm}^{- 2} \times \dfrac{{\left(0 . 02m\right)}^{2}}{20m} \times A \\ & ⇒ & A = \dfrac{2 \times 80J \times 20}{2 . 0 \times {10}^{11} \times 4 \times {10}^{- 4}{Nm}^{- 1}} \\ & = & 4 \times {10}^{- 5}{m}^{2} \times \dfrac{{10}^{6}{mm}^{2}}{1{m}^{2}} \\ & = & 40{mm}^{2}\end{cases}$

questions.solution:
The relations of Young's modulus, $Y$, bulk modulus, $K$, the modulus of rigidity, $η$ and Poisson's ratio, $\sigma$ are given as

$⇒ 2η\left(1 + \sigma\right) = 3K\left(1 - 2\sigma\right)$

$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{A}_1 \ell_1=\mathrm{A}_2 \ell_2 \Rightarrow \ell_2=\frac{\mathrm{A}_1 \ell_1}{\mathrm{~A}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{A} \times \ell_1}{3 \mathrm{~A}}=\frac{\ell_1}{3} \Rightarrow \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}=3 \\
& \Delta \mathrm{x}_1=\frac{\mathrm{F}_1}{\mathrm{~A} \gamma} \times \ell_1 \\
& \Delta \mathrm{x}_2=\frac{\mathrm{F}_2}{3 \mathrm{~A} \gamma} \ell_2 \\

& \frac{\mathrm{F}_2}{3 \mathrm{~A} \gamma} \ell_2=\frac{\mathrm{F}_1}{\mathrm{~A} \gamma} \ell_1 \\
& \left.\mathrm{~F}_2=3 \mathrm{~F}_1 \times \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}=3 \mathrm{~F}_1 \times 3=\mathrm{i}\right)
\end{aligned}
$
